findings.paper_title: 5c Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Cyber security controls remain incomplete; Incident Response Plan still being finalized
findings.detail: Despite progress on implementing prior recommendations from an advisory audit on IT Incident Management and Security, the council states "the ever changing IT environment means that there is still work to be completed to manage the inherent risks." The Cyber Incident Response Plan is still being finalized for adoption by Corporate Leadership Team.
findings.matters: Cyber incidents could disrupt council operations, corrupt or expose financial data, and disrupt service delivery
findings.figures: No completion date given for Incident Response Plan; no timeline for completing cyber work
findings.quote: Although good progress has been made on implementing the recommendations that were made as part of an advisory audit on IT Incident Management and Security, the ever changing IT environment means that there is still work to be completed to manage the inherent risks.

findings.paper_title: 5c Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Procurement control weaknesses persist despite 2024/25 action marked complete; Partial Assurance audit rating issued
findings.detail: Procurement received a Partial Assurance internal audit rating in 2024/25 but the action was marked complete. Procurement remains a listed governance issue for 2025/26, with ongoing review work to assess compliance with Contract Procedure Rules and Procurement Act 2023, and management of the Welland Procurement Service Level Agreement.
findings.matters: Procurement control failures affect value for money, fraud risk, and proper use of public funds; the issue persisting despite being marked resolved suggests either incomplete remediation or recurring problems
findings.figures: Partial Assurance rating in 2024/25; continuing as active issue into 2025/26
findings.quote: Four Partial Assurance internal audit reports have been issued relating to the controls and processes in place during the 2024/25 financial year. These reports were in respect of Procurement, Landlord Licensing, Sickness Absence and Safeguarding.

findings.paper_title: 5c Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Two of four audit follow-up reviews in 2024/25 showed poor or little progress on implementing prior recommendations
findings.detail: Follow-up audits on implementation of 2024/25 recommendations resulted in "two reasonable progress opinions (positive) one little progress (negative) opinion, and one poor progress (negative) opinion." The council has identified this as a 2025/26 governance issue, committing to strengthen arrangements for timely and effective implementation of audit recommendations through enhanced monitoring.
findings.matters: Non-implementation of audit recommendations indicates control gaps persist; weak follow-through on audit action plans is a red flag for governance quality
findings.figures: 4 follow-up reviews: 2 reasonable progress, 1 little progress, 1 poor progress
findings.quote: We have performed four follow up reviews during the year to follow up all actions raised as part of the 2024/25 internal audit plan, which resulted in two reasonable progress opinions (positive) one little progress (negative) opinion, and one poor progress (negative) opinion.

findings.paper_title: 5c Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: External audit identified weaknesses in management review processes for statutory financial reporting
findings.detail: External audit found insufficient management review processes in place to support preparation of draft financial statements. The council has committed to establish sufficient quality review procedures to ensure statutory financial reporting accurately reflects underlying transactions. This was the specific exception cited in the auditor's qualified governance opinion.
findings.matters: Financial statement reliability is foundational to lending decisions; external audit flagged this as a governance weakness requiring correction
findings.figures: External Auditor Value for Money opinion: "Except for the matter relating to financial reporting" the council's governance arrangements are adequate
findings.quote: A number of recommendations have been made by external audit to address weaknesses in the management review processes in respect of the Council's statutory reporting. These include sufficient review processes being established and put in place to support the preparation of draft financial statements to ensure sufficient quality review procedures are set up to support accurate statutory financial reporting that this is reflective of the underlying transactions.

findings.paper_title: 4b - Appendix 1 - BDC Annual Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £32.6m against revised budget of £94.6m—a 65% underspend
findings.detail: Capital delivery was far below budget: General Fund £17.4m of £55.7m (69% miss); HRA £15.2m of £38.9m (61% miss). Despite revised budgets, neither fund had unfinanced capital expenditure, suggesting projects did not proceed rather than being financing-constrained.
findings.matters: Persistent large variances between budgeted and delivered capital indicate planning or execution challenges, not just one-off delays. A lender must assess whether capital strategies are realistic and whether the council has the capacity to deliver capital programmes.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure: 2024-25 actual £21.1m; 2025-26 revised budget £94.6m; actual £32.6m
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure TOTAL 21,083 94,650* 32,561

findings.paper_title: 4b - Appendix 1 - BDC Annual Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital Grants Unapplied fell from £41.1m to £31.2m—consuming £9.9m of finite resources in one year
findings.detail: The council's available capital grants declined by £9.9m in 2025-26. These are one-time government resources that must be applied to capital use and cannot be replenished. As they deplete, future capital funding becomes more dependent on borrowing—a risk in the current environment of elevated PWLB rates (5%+).
findings.matters: Declining finite grant resources restrict the council's ability to self-finance capital and increase borrowing dependency. This forces reliance on market borrowing at rates the council cannot control, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital Grants Unapplied: £41,062k (31 Mar 2025) to £31,178k (31 Mar 2026); annual burn of £9.9m
findings.quote: Capital Grants Unapplied 41,062 31,178

findings.paper_title: 4b - Appendix 1 - BDC Annual Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: £200k expected credit loss allowance recognised on £3.2m loan to subsidiary Bersahill Limited
findings.detail: The council has recognised a £200k expected credit loss allowance on a £3.2m loan to Bersahill, its wholly-owned property development subsidiary. The council is relying on expected sale proceeds from plots at Madison Court to support loan repayment, indicating credit deterioration and exposure to property market risk.
findings.matters: Direct subsidiary lending represents concentration of risk on a non-core activity whose financial position is deteriorating. A lender needs to assess whether subsidiary losses could impair council finances or whether this reflects over-commitment beyond core services.
findings.figures: £3.2m loan principal; £200k expected credit loss allowance (6% of loan value)
findings.quote: A review of the outstanding loan balance from Bersahill has been undertaken, which has required the Council to make an allowance for potential losses of £200,000 (referred to as the expected credit loss allowance).

findings.paper_title: 4a - Finance and Performance Monitoring Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Awaab's Law compliance driving significant damp and mould remediation costs as part of £709k HRA deficit
findings.detail: The new Awaab's Law requirement to remediate damp and mould in social housing is generating material additional repair and maintenance costs as part of the HRA overspend. These are ongoing compliance obligations that will persist into future years and represent a structural cost pressure on the housing budget.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs that cannot be avoided represent a permanent budget pressure. Failure to remediate exposes the council to regulatory action and litigation risk. This cost may not be fully absorbed by the current HRA business model.
findings.figures: Damp proofing costs embedded in £561k repairs maintenance overspend and £709k HRA deficit
findings.quote: The HRA outturn is an adverse variance of £709k. This is primarily due to increased repairs and maintenance and damp proofing costs associated with the new Awaab's Law

findings.paper_title: 4a - Finance and Performance Monitoring Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Property income underachievement of £135k from vacant industrial estate units and reduced community centre lettings
findings.detail: Finance and Property services missed income targets by £135k due to vacant units on the industrial estate and reduced letting income from community centres. Growth and Economic Prosperity also experienced void and reduced income issues at The Priory Centre (£174k additional cost) and CCTV maintenance pressures (£244k), pointing to broader property portfolio challenges.
findings.matters: Unplanned income shortfalls force service cuts or reserve draws. Rising vacancy rates and declining commercial lettings suggest the council's property portfolio is not generating expected returns, affecting financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £135k income underachievement in Finance and Property; £174k void costs at Priory Centre; £244k CCTV maintenance
findings.quote: An underachievement of income (£135k) mainly due to vacant industrial estate units and reduced letting income from community centres.

findings.paper_title: 4a - Finance and Performance Monitoring Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: £38.3m capital programme carry-forwards, including £17.7m Levelling Up Partnership delays and £13.2m Priory Centre redevelopment slippage
findings.detail: The council is reproffiling major regeneration projects into 2026-27 and beyond, citing delays with planning permissions, contract completion, and programme delivery. Key delays include Levelling Up Partnership Fund (£17.7m), Priory Centre redevelopment (£13.2m), Bersahill property purchase (£2.5m), and Public Sector Decarbonisation (£1.3m). The council notes potential challenges to delivery capacity for the full 2026-27 programme.
findings.matters: Large-scale project delays signal delivery and project management risks, particularly for externally funded regeneration schemes where deadline extensions may not be available. Slippage also delays expected income and economic benefits.
findings.figures: £38.3m carry-forward from 2025-26 to 2026-27; Levelling Up Partnership £17.7m; Priory Centre £13.2m; Bersahill £2.5m
findings.quote: Proposed year-end budget movements (38.3) 40.0 1.7 ... We are expecting slippage on this programme meaning some budgets will need carrying forward into 2026/27 financial year.

findings.paper_title: 4a - Finance and Performance Monitoring Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: HRA deficit of £709k, worsened by £455k since Q3, driven by damp proofing and void costs
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account swung from a £254k deficit forecast in Q3 to £709k at outturn. Repairs and maintenance overspent by £561k, primarily from Awaab's Law compliance costs (damp proofing) and sustained pressure on voids. The council's rent arrears stand at £370,723.74, and it is managing 388 total voids with an average relet time of 135.72 days for standard voids (flagged red).
findings.matters: Growing HRA deficits indicate the council's housing service is structurally under pressure and cannot cover its repair obligations from rental income. This affects debt serviceability and the council's ability to maintain housing stock.
findings.figures: £709k deficit, £561k repairs overspend, 388 voids, 135.72 days relet time, £370,723.74 rent arrears
findings.quote: The HRA outturn is an adverse variance of £709k. This is primarily due to increased repairs and maintenance and damp proofing costs associated with the new Awaab's Law and ongoing pressure on the housing voids allowance

findings.paper_title: 6g - Corporate Risk Managament Q4, 2025-26
findings.headline: Persistent staffing shortages limiting service delivery
findings.detail: Insufficient staff to deliver council services and goals is identified as C5 (amber), explicitly noted as a national recruitment and skills problem. No improvement from previous quarter. The paper does not quantify vacancy levels or service impact.
findings.matters: Staff shortages limit a council's capacity to deliver services and generate revenue; persistent amber rating suggests the problem is not being resolved.
findings.figures: Risk #5, rating C5 (amber), unchanged from Q3
findings.quote: Insufficient number of staff to be able to deliver the Council's services / goals. National problem with recruitment and skills shortage

findings.paper_title: 6g - Corporate Risk Managament Q4, 2025-26
findings.headline: Savings proposals risk removed after being brought to target level
findings.detail: The council removes a red-rated savings risk (Risk #1, previously D4) from the corporate register because 'current risk and target risk now align'. This signals either achievement of planned savings or acceptance of revised targets, but the document does not specify which.
findings.matters: Movement on savings proposals is material to credit assessment; removal suggests either budget shortfall has been closed or expectations have been reset downward.
findings.figures: Risk #1: D4 (red) → now removed on alignment with target
findings.quote: It is proposed that the risk for 'Savings proposals identified through the budget review work not being achieved' is now removed from the Corporate Risk Register as its current risk and target risk now align.

findings.paper_title: 6g - Corporate Risk Managament Q4, 2025-26
findings.headline: Supported accommodation subsidy loss creating budget pressures
findings.detail: The council identifies increased supported accommodation numbers as causing budget pressures specifically through loss of subsidies. This is rated C5 (amber) and unchanged from the previous quarter. No financial quantum is provided.
findings.matters: This represents a direct demand-led budget pressure from changing demographics and withdrawal of external funding; a lender would need to know the scale to assess council finances.
findings.figures: Risk #4, rating C5 (amber), unchanged from Q3
findings.quote: Increase in the number of supported accommodation creating budget pressures on the Council due to a loss of subsidies

findings.paper_title: 6g - Corporate Risk Managament Q4, 2025-26
findings.headline: Long-term financial integrity remains an amber risk with no improvement
findings.detail: The council's long-term financial integrity is identified as a C5 (amber) corporate risk, unchanged from the previous quarter. No detail is given on what constitutes this risk or the nature of the financial sustainability concern.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the specific threats to the council's financial viability. Persistence of this risk at amber level across two quarters signals an unresolved concern.
findings.figures: Risk #9, rating C5 (amber), unchanged from Q3
findings.quote: Long term financial integrity of the Council

findings.paper_title: 6f - Assesment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation creates structural uncertainty, with full proposals due November 2026.
findings.detail: The council is subject to planned local government reorganisation under the English Devolution White Paper (16 December 2024). The Minister requested interim plans by March 2025 and full reorganisation proposals by 28 November 2026. The council has assessed the impact on going concern but reorganisation could alter service delivery, governance structures, and potentially asset holdings.
findings.matters: Unresolved structural reorganisation creates medium-term uncertainty about the council's legal existence, service scope, and asset base—material factors for long-term lending decisions and medium-term financial planning.
findings.figures: Full proposals due 28 November 2026; interim plans were due 21 March 2025
findings.quote: The Minister requested interim plans to be submitted by 21st March 2025, and full proposals to be submitted by 28th November.

findings.paper_title: 6f - Assesment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Going concern opinion is limited to twelve months, not the standard indefinite assumption.
findings.detail: The section 151 officer's conclusion explicitly states the council 'can continue to operate as a going concern for a period of twelve months from the date of signing the audit opinion', rather than the standard indefinite going concern basis. This time-limited assessment reflects the identified financial risks and planning horizon constraints.
findings.matters: A time-limited going concern opinion is a material audit constraint that requires annual reassessment and signals auditor-identified financial risk; lenders typically expect unconditional going concern status.
findings.figures: Going concern assessed for 12 months from audit opinion date
findings.quote: It is considered that having regard to the Council's arrangements, and to specific factors highlighted in this report, the Council can continue to operate as a going concern for a period of twelve months from the date of signing the audit opinion

findings.paper_title: 6f - Assesment of Going Concern
findings.headline: The council acknowledges limited reserves and warns that emergency savings plans may be required in a worst-case scenario.
findings.detail: Despite general reserves of £4.01m and earmarked reserves of £11.09m, the section 151 officer explicitly states the council cannot be complacent and that timely action is imperative. The conclusion warns that emergency savings plans may need to be implemented if normal efficiency measures do not deliver sufficient savings.
findings.matters: A finance director's own characterisation of reserves as non-substantial and contingency planning for emergency cuts indicates awareness of limited financial headroom and dependency on delivery of discretionary savings plans.
findings.figures: General reserves £4.01m; earmarked reserves £11.09m; minimum general reserves threshold £1.0m
findings.quote: The Council does not have substantial reserves upon which to rely and therefore cannot be complacent in seeking efficiencies to deliver any savings required. Timely action will remain imperative to address risk and, in a worst case scenario, emergency savings plans may need to be implemented.

findings.paper_title: 6f - Assesment of Going Concern
findings.headline: A budget gap emerges beyond the three-year MTFP planning horizon, creating post-2028/29 financial uncertainty.
findings.detail: The council can produce balanced budgets through 2026/27 to 2028/29 with savings proposals in place, but after that period there is a budget gap caused by funding reform uncertainty. Work to address the remaining gap will continue but has not yet been resolved. This represents a forward-looking deficit without a current funding solution.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of multi-year financial plans; an identified shortfall three years out that lacks a funding solution represents refinancing risk and potential dependency on emergency measures.
findings.figures: Balanced budget for 2026/27 to 2028/29; budget gap thereafter; 2026/27 net spending £25.44m with 2.99% council tax increase
findings.quote: The Council's latest Medium Term Financial Plan indicates that a balanced budget can be produced for the next three years and thereafter the financial uncertainty of funding reforms means that there is a budget gap.

findings.paper_title: 6d - Governance Action Plan Update (Annual Governance Statement 2024-25)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation preparation underway with final submission submitted and dedicated finance, legal and communications workstreams now operational
findings.detail: Following the English Devolution White Paper in December 2024, the council submitted its LGR proposal on time. Dedicated workstreams including finance are now operational with data sharing and internal capacity building underway.
findings.matters: LGR represents material structural change requiring explicit governance and financial risk management. The council notes LGR requires reflection of transitional governance, risk management, and financial sustainability implications.
findings.figures: Final LGR submission submitted on time; dedicated finance workstream operational
findings.quote: LGR requires councils to explicitly reflect transitional governance, risk management, and financial implications within the Annual Governance Statement, ensuring that the impact of structural change is transparently articulated and properly managed.

findings.paper_title: 6d - Governance Action Plan Update (Annual Governance Statement 2024-25)
findings.headline: Commercial asset portfolio being transferred to S80 Partnership Limited with Harrison Drive and Ashvale Road estates transferred in 2025/26 and parking tariffs increased from April 2026
findings.detail: Harrison Drive and Ashvale Road industrial estates successfully transferred to S80 Partnership Limited in 2025/26, with additional sites identified for transfer. New car parking tariffs were implemented from 1st April 2026 following finalisation of the Car Parking Strategy.
findings.matters: Asset monetization and income generation initiatives directly support the council's financial sustainability and capital receipt generation, relevant to its ongoing financial position.
findings.figures: Harrison Drive and Ashvale Road transferred 2025/26; new parking tariffs from 1st April 2026
findings.quote: Harrison Drive and Ashvale Road industrial estates have successfully transferred in 2025/26, marking a key milestone. Additional sites have been identified and are undergoing preparation for transfer, supporting a streamlined approach to asset management and long-term financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 6d - Governance Action Plan Update (Annual Governance Statement 2024-25)
findings.headline: Four Partial Assurance internal audit reports issued covering procurement, landlord licensing, sickness absence and safeguarding
findings.detail: During 2024/25, internal audit issued four reports with Partial Assurance ratings. These covered procurement (also identified separately as a significant governance issue), landlord licensing, sickness absence and safeguarding. All recommendations have been agreed and are being implemented with follow-up audits planned.
findings.matters: Partial Assurance ratings indicate control weaknesses requiring management action. Procurement control weaknesses are particularly relevant to procurement risk and financial controls.
findings.figures: Four Partial Assurance audit reports issued; Procurement also separately identified as a significant governance issue
findings.quote: Four Partial Assurance internal audit reports have been issued relating to the controls and processes in place during the 2024/25 financial year. These reports were in respect of Procurement, Landlord Licensing, Sickness Absence and Safeguarding.

findings.paper_title: 6d - Governance Action Plan Update (Annual Governance Statement 2024-25)
findings.headline: External audit identified weaknesses in financial statement review processes that required improvements to management review procedures
findings.detail: External audit made recommendations to address weaknesses in management review processes for statutory financial reporting. The council has progressed a walk-through test and advanced its consistency checker. These improvements will feed into 2025/26 accounts preparation.
findings.matters: Weaknesses in financial statement review procedures directly affect the quality and accuracy of statutory reporting that lenders rely on to assess the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Weakness identified in management review processes for draft financial statements
findings.quote: A number of recommendations have been made by external audit to address weaknesses in the management review processes in respect of the Council's statutory reporting. These include sufficient review processes being established and put in place to support the preparation of draft financial statements

findings.paper_title: 6a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Annual Internal Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Only reasonable assurance (not substantial) could be taken on most audit reviews; 78% of assurance opinions were at the middle rather than highest confidence level.
findings.detail: Nine assurance reviews were completed: two resulted in 'substantial assurance' (22%), seven in 'reasonable assurance' (78%). Reasonable assurance indicates that controls are adequate and the framework is appropriately designed, but leaves more room for failure than the highest confidence level.
findings.matters: Lenders assess council control maturity through audit opinions. Reasonable assurance across the majority of areas suggests controls are not as robust as they could be, consistent with the pattern of implementation failures noted above.
findings.figures: 2 of 9 reviews: substantial assurance (22%); 7 of 9 reviews: reasonable assurance (78%).
findings.quote: in seven reviews (78%) we concluded that reasonable assurance could be taken in relation to the design and application of the control frameworks in place

findings.paper_title: 6a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Annual Internal Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: The council remains vulnerable to identified audit risks where prior recommendations have not been implemented.
findings.detail: The report explicitly states that where audit management actions remain outstanding, the council is 'still vulnerable to the risks identified.' A total of 150 management actions were agreed in 2025/26, and the failure to implement prior-year actions means risks remediated elsewhere continue to expose the organisation.
findings.matters: Outstanding control weaknesses create unmitigated risk exposure. A lender needs assurance that identified financial and operational risks are being actively addressed; a pattern of inaction suggests risks may compound.
findings.figures: 150 total actions agreed in 2025/26; at least 20 actions not implemented in Follow Ups 1 and 4 alone.
findings.quote: where actions remain outstanding, the council are still vulnerable to the risks identified

findings.paper_title: 6a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Annual Internal Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Two audit follow-ups resulted in negative opinions, demonstrating a governance weakness in implementing prior audit recommendations.
findings.detail: The council's follow-up review of 2024/25 audit actions shows a pattern of implementation failure. Two of four follow-up reviews (covering 64 separate actions) resulted in negative opinions: one 'little progress' finding (11 of 28 actions implemented) and one 'poor progress' finding (13 of 36 actions implemented). The auditors explicitly identify this as 'a governance weakness.'
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether the council can execute on commitments it makes. Repeated failure to implement audit recommendations suggests either capacity constraints or governance problems that could affect broader operational delivery.
findings.figures: Follow Up 1: 11 of 28 actions implemented (39%). Follow Up 4: 13 of 36 actions implemented (36%); 10 of 36 not implemented.
findings.quote: two of these resulted in negative opinions which demonstrates a governance weakness

findings.paper_title: 1a - Report - Housing Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2030-31
findings.headline: The 2026/27 programme requires £22.21m of new borrowing, with ongoing borrowing dependency through 2030/31
findings.detail: Of the £30.06m planned 2026/27 spend, £22.21m (74%) is to be funded by borrowing. This is the first year of a 5-year programme totalling £94.287m. As RTB receipts disappear, borrowing will remain the only significant funding source, and the council's HRA debt will grow substantially.
findings.matters: For a lender, the trajectory matters: rising debt plus falling income streams plus constrained new-build capacity equals deteriorating debt serviceability. The council is explicitly warning Cabinet to consider the long-term borrowing impact on HRA affordability.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £22.21m borrowing from £30.06m total; 5-year programme: £94.287m (detailed year-by-year split in Appendix 1, not provided)
findings.quote: The longer-term funding of the Housing Capital Programme will be substantially dependant on borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 1a - Report - Housing Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Building cost inflation is eroding budget—planned works may not be deliverable in scheduled years
findings.detail: The paper notes that rising construction costs mean unit prices in the stock condition survey are already inflated, and the council may be unable to deliver all planned works in their scheduled years. The council intends to use 5-year smoothing to manage this, but this delays urgent works.
findings.matters: Budget slippage is a sign of either insufficient funding or cost control failure. If works drift beyond year 5, the council's 30-year HRA plan becomes unreliable, and the backlog of deferred maintenance could become a future liability.
findings.figures: 5-year capital programme: £94.287m; 2026/27 allocated £30.06m
findings.quote: The unit prices identified within the surveys, have been inflated due to rising building cost inflation and as a result this may mean that not all works will be achievable in the exact year that the work becomes due and therefore smoothing of programmes will ensure that work is still carried out in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: 1a - Report - Housing Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Government revision to Decent Homes Standard (outcome pending) could impose unfunded investment requirements
findings.detail: A consultation on a revised Decent Homes Standard took place in 2025, with outcome unknown. The paper states the revision will include addressing energy efficiency and the Social Housing Regulator's Quality and Safety Standard applies from 1 April 2024. If the standard is tightened, the council's current plan (based on stock surveys) could become insufficient without identifying additional funding.
findings.matters: This is a latent unfunded liability. If the standard is revised upward, the council may face a gap between planned spend and required spend. Lenders need to understand potential hidden costs.
findings.figures: Currently 97.55% of stock meets Decent Homes Standard (as at 1 January 2026); 2.45% non-compliant
findings.quote: The Social Housing Regulation Act 2023 commits Government to reviewing and increasing the Standard including addressing energy efficiency measures, and a consultation on a revised Decent Homes Standard took place during 2025, the outcome of which is not yet known.

findings.paper_title: 1a - Report - Housing Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2030-31
findings.headline: New-build provision has been deferred to prioritise existing stock maintenance and meet compliance obligations
findings.detail: Future new build and new housing provision is explicitly deprioritised in order to maintain existing stock and meet regulatory compliance. The paper states the council "will prioritise works to the existing housing stock, meet our landlord compliance obligations and ensure sufficient revenue monies to continue to deliver high quality housing management". This trade-off suggests the HRA is constrained.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender needs to know that the council is rationing investment—choosing between repairs and growth is a sign of financial pressure, not stability. It also increases risk of future catch-up investment needs.
findings.figures: 2026/27 expenditure: £30.06m, with no significant new build; £2.66m provisional allocation for acquisitions only
findings.quote: Further new build provision has been deferred within the Housing Capital Programme in order to prioritise works to the existing housing stock, meet our landlord compliance obligations and ensure sufficient revenue monies to continue to deliver high quality housing management and maintenance services

findings.paper_title: 1a - Report - Housing Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2030-31
findings.headline: 120-unit Radford Street development abandoned in July 2024 on the grounds of unviability
findings.detail: The council's own new-build housing scheme was cancelled because of inflation and unviability—the economic case collapsed. The site is now being disposed of at market value with only 30 units of affordable housing negotiated back in lieu. This is a strategic reversal and signals that the council has already hit affordability limits.
findings.matters: If the council's own development became unviable mid-plan, the HRA's ability to invest is tighter than the budget suggests. It also raises questions about whether planned acquisitions and refurbishments will proceed as scheduled.
findings.figures: 120 units abandoned; 30 units acquired from developer instead; disposal to generate small capital receipt
findings.quote: the proposed development of 120 units of new build council housing at Radford Street were re-considered and on 24th July 2024, Cabinet agreed not to proceed with the full re-development of the site, due to unviability issues.

findings.paper_title: 1a - Report - Housing Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Right to Buy receipts will fall from £0.6m annual retention to zero, forcing £22.21m additional borrowing in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: Sales are forecast to drop to 6 properties per annum (from 50 in 2025/26) following the November 2024 policy change that capped discounts at £24,000. This ends the council's ability to retain surplus RTB proceeds, which has historically offset borrowing. The paper explicitly states: from 2026/27 onwards "receipts will be too low to generate anything", meaning the council must either borrow more or defer works.
findings.matters: A major revenue stream is disappearing while capital commitments remain fixed. Lenders and the finance director need to know whether the HRA can service additional debt without revenue deterioration.
findings.figures: £0.6m annual retention drops to zero from 2026/27; RTB sales forecast 6 per annum vs. historical 50; balance of unused 1-4-1 receipts: £3.36m at 1 April 2025
findings.quote: From 2026/27 the receipts will be too low to generate anything.

findings.paper_title: 7a - Report - General Fund Budget 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: National Living Wage rising 4.1% to £12.71 from April 2026, exceeding budgeted general pay award of 3%, creating unbudgeted cost pressure in care and leisure services
findings.detail: The budget assumes a general pay award of 3% for 2026/27, falling to 2.5% and 2% in following years. However, the National Living Wage is rising 4.1% to £12.71 per hour from April 2026. The council acknowledges this mismatch has 'significant implications for local authorities, particularly in areas such as care services, leisure, and contracted services, where a large proportion of staff are paid at or near the NLW.' This cost inflation is unbudgeted and will either reduce service capacity or require cuts elsewhere.
findings.matters: Care and leisure services often operate on tight margins and income-dependent budgets. If staffing costs rise faster than anticipated, the council will face either service cuts or budget overruns that reduce reported reserves.
findings.figures: National Living Wage increase: 4.1% to £12.71/hour from April 2026. General pay award 2026/27: 3%; 2027/28: 2.5%; 2028/29: 2.0%. Differential in first year: +1.1% on NLW-dependent workforce.
findings.quote: This uplift will have significant implications for local authorities, particularly in areas such as care services, leisure, and contracted services, where a large proportion of staff are paid at or near the NLW. Budget planning for 2026/27 will need to account for this increase, alongside other inflationary pressures.

findings.paper_title: 7a - Report - General Fund Budget 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Population aged 65+ rising 24.6% over 2011-2021 decade, creating growing demand pressure on social care, housing, and homelessness services
findings.detail: Bassetlaw experienced a 24.6% increase in residents aged 65 and over between 2011 and 2021, 'creating future pressures on health, social care, and housing services.' ONS projections show total population rising to 123,400 by 2026, with the aging trend continuing. This is particularly acute in a district ranked 111th out of 296 local authorities for deprivation, where households have limited means to fund private care. The council's Core Spending Power is declining, not rising, making it increasingly difficult to absorb demand growth.
findings.matters: Demand for statutory services (particularly social care, housing, and homelessness) will rise faster than overall population growth. If demand growth outpaces the declining budget, the council will be forced to cut services or increase contributions to reserves, worsening the funding cliff edge after 2029.
findings.figures: Population aged 65+ increase: 24.6% (2011-2021). Projected total population: 123,400 by 2026 (vs 117,800 in 2021). Deprivation ranking: 111th out of 296 local authorities (IMD 2025 score 22.540). CSP per head: £171.11 (2028/29), down 4.3% from £178.76 (2025/26).
findings.quote: a 24.6% increase in residents aged 65 and over which signals a significant demographic shift, creating future pressures on health, social care, and housing services.

findings.paper_title: 7a - Report - General Fund Budget 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation from April 2028 creates unquantified transitional costs and successor authority funding uncertainty
findings.detail: The council is preparing for creation of a new unitary authority from 1 April 2028. While potentially offering longer-term efficiency gains, the transition creates immediate material costs. The council acknowledges the need for a 'dedicated Project Management Office' requiring either secondment of existing staff (creating backfill pressures) or recruitment of temporary resources. Beyond staffing, there will be 'one-off costs associated with harmonising systems, aligning policies, and managing contractual obligations'. The successor authority's post-2029 funding position remains uncertain. The Council is appropriating £1m per year to a new Capital Financing Reserve partly to manage LGR transition costs.
findings.matters: A lender must assess governance stability. The transition to a new unitary authority introduces operational risk, cost uncertainty, and unknown funding arrangements post-April 2028. Service continuity and financial control could be disrupted during the change.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Reserve: £1m appropriated per year from 2026/27. Unquantified: programme management office costs, system harmonisation, policy alignment, redundancy and redeployment. Total General Fund reserves projected: £17.265m (March 2026), £16.4m (March 2028), £16.2m (March 2029).
findings.quote: Establishing a dedicated Project Management Office will be essential to coordinate activities across multiple workstreams, including finance, HR, ICT, and service integration. This may require either seconding existing staff, creating backfill pressures, or recruiting temporary resources, both of which will increase costs during the transition phase.

findings.paper_title: 7a - Report - General Fund Budget 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Service budget savings becoming harder to deliver, with employee costs at two-thirds of spend limiting flexibility to cut further without workforce reductions
findings.detail: The council reports that 'identifying new savings each year is becoming increasingly difficult, as service budgets have been reduced over several years, limiting flexibility to respond to emerging pressures once the budget is set.' Analysis shows employee costs are 'nearly 2/3 of direct service costs attributable to the General Fund'. This means non-employee savings opportunities are exhausted and future savings must come from workforce reductions. The council states transformation 'is no longer optional, it is central to the Council's ability to adapt'.
findings.matters: If income targets slip or demand pressures emerge, the council has limited ability to find offsetting savings without significant redundancy costs and service disruption. This reduces financial flexibility and increases downside risk.
findings.figures: Employee costs: approximately 67% of direct General Fund service costs. Savings delivered 2025/26: 92% of target achieved (£1.0m delivered, £1.1m target). Budget gap 2026/27-2028/29 filled through: £1.571m (2026/27) and £0.660m (2027/28) in appropriations to reserves.
findings.quote: Identifying new savings each year is becoming increasingly difficult, as service budgets have been reduced over several years, limiting flexibility to respond to emerging pressures once the budget is set. Transformation is no longer optional, it is central to the Council's ability to adapt, modernise, and meet the needs of residents in a financially constrained environment.

findings.paper_title: 7a - Report - General Fund Budget 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Council heavily dependent on Council Tax increases to offset central government funding cuts, constrained by weak tax base of 49% Band A properties
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Allocation is falling from 55.9% of Core Spending Power (2026/27) to 41.4% (2028/29), forcing increasing reliance on Council Tax. Bassetlaw has structural revenue constraints: 49% of properties fall into Band A (the lowest band) versus only 23.7% nationally. This weak tax base limits revenue-raising capacity and forces a higher Band D charge to compensate. Bassetlaw's Council Tax per head is ranked 52nd out of 164 District Councils and is forecast to remain 20% below the district average through 2028/29 despite a 2.99% annual increase.
findings.matters: A council with nearly half its properties in the lowest tax band cannot easily raise additional revenue without triggering affordability crises for residents. It is politically constrained at a time of cost-of-living pressure and has no fallback mechanism if other income assumptions fail.
findings.figures: Band A properties: 49% (vs 23.7% nationally). Council Tax gearing: 38.7% (2026/27) rising to 42.3% (2028/29), or 48.2% excluding temporary grants. CSP per capita: £173.47 (2026/27), falling to £171.11 (2028/29). District council average: projected £186.69 by 2028/29.
findings.quote: nearly half of Bassetlaw's properties (49%) fall within Band A, more than double the national average of 23.7% for English local authorities. This significant variance highlights the district's disproportionate concentration of lower-banded properties compared to councils across England.

findings.paper_title: 7a - Report - General Fund Budget 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Fair Funding Allocation falling 33.6% from £13.3m (2025/26 baseline) to £8.8m (2028/29) when temporary grants end, with no stated mitigation plan
findings.detail: The new Fair Funding Review provides temporary protection through a funding floor (£2.2m) and Recovery Grant (£0.4m) lasting to March 2029. Once these end, the Fair Funding Allocation drops from £13.308m to £8.833m. The council explicitly states that 'it is not clear how this funding cliff edge will be handled going into the next multi-year settlement' and that assumptions are 'set at a worst-case scenario'. The report acknowledges 'uncertainty remains beyond April 2029, when the next spending review is announced' but offers no contingency strategy beyond hoping for better outcomes.
findings.matters: A lender must know whether the council can survive the loss of £2.6m in annual funding. This cliff edge is certain to arrive but the funding solution is not. The council will be forced into either further service cuts, large Council Tax increases, or reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: Fair Funding Allocation 2025/26: £13.308m; 2026/27: £11.958m; 2027/28: £10.430m; 2028/29: £8.833m. Funding Floor (95% income protection): £0m (2026/27), £1.010m (2027/28), £2.185m (2028/29). Recovery Grant: £0.453m per year through March 2029, then expected to end.
findings.quote: it is not clear how this funding 'cliff edge' will be handled going into the next multi-year settlement so assumptions in this report are set at a worst-case scenario

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance savings of £1.25m—£1.875m depend on completion of in-progress reforms with no guarantee of delivery
findings.detail: The HRA budget assumes savings of 10% (£1.25m in 2026/27, rising to £1.875m from 2027/28 onwards) from non-staffing repair and maintenance costs following a detailed review completed in November 2024. Work to implement these recommendations is 'ongoing' and a revised Repairs Policy will come to Cabinet on 10 March 2026. The budget assumes these savings happen, but implementation is not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: If repairs reform does not deliver the expected savings, the HRA deficit would widen, deepening the later-year reserve shortfall.
findings.figures: 10% of current non-staffing repair costs: £1.25m in 2026/27, £1.875m from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Following the Repairs and Maintenance Review and time to implement the improvement plan, the HRA budget assumes that up to 15% of the current repair and maintenance revenue spend on non-staffing costs can be saved. This is assumed to be 10%, or £1.25m at 2025/26 prices in 2026/27 and £1.875m savings per annum at 2025/26 prices from 2027/28 onwards.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Stock condition survey to be refreshed starting January 2026; current investment plan based on outdated assumptions
findings.detail: The council notes that current investment assumptions for years 10-30 of the business plan are based on a 'particularly heavy stock investment need in later years', but a new stock condition survey was just procured and will commence January 2026. This suggests the investment profile in the business plan may be inaccurate and could require material revision upwards or downwards.
findings.matters: A revised stock condition survey may reveal that planned capital investment is insufficient (requiring more borrowing) or that the current debt/investment profile is not sustainable.
findings.figures: No numbers yet; survey commences January 2026.
findings.quote: The current plan assumes a particularly heavy stock investment need in later years; however, a refreshed stock condition survey has just been procured and which commences in January 2026, will provide an updated understanding of the future needs for investment.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Disrepair claims increasing while new regulatory requirements compress response timescales
findings.detail: The Housing Service is experiencing both an increase in demand for repairs and an increase in disrepair claims, which must be responded to within stringent timescales. Combined with new Awaab's Law obligations, this creates a compounding service demand and cost pressure.
findings.matters: Rising disrepair claims indicate potential historic underinvestment in maintenance or more aggressive tenant pursuit of remedies, both of which signal latent liabilities.
findings.figures: Numbers not quantified in budget.
findings.quote: The Housing Service is seeing an increased demand for repairs and an increase in disrepair claims, which have to be responded to within stringent timescales.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Awaab's Law implementation creating new compliance obligations with 24-hour inspection timescales
findings.detail: Awaab's Law came into force 27 October 2025, requiring councils to inspect properties for hazards (starting with damp and mould) within 24 hours where a tenant has underlying health needs, issue a written report within 48 hours, and start repair work within 7 days. The paper notes this has resulted in increased reports of hazards and created additional burden on staff, requiring additional resources to be introduced in 2025.
findings.matters: New statutory compliance obligations with very tight timescales create revenue pressure (more repairs staff, faster response) that may not be fully budgeted.
findings.figures: 24-hour inspection requirement, 48-hour reporting, 7-day repair start requirement
findings.quote: Awaab's Law, which was introduced on 27 October 2025, has resulted in an increase in reports of hazards – currently damp and mould, with further hazards being introduced in 2026 and 2027 (under the HHSRS) where a tenant has underlying health needs these will need to be inspected within 24 hours, a written report issued of what work will be undertaken within 48 hours and repair work started within 7 days.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Regulatory exposure shifted from £5k cap to unlimited fines for RSH Consumer Standards non-compliance
findings.detail: The council notes a significant change in regulatory enforcement: the Regulator of Social Housing moved from a £5,000 cap for non-compliance to unlimited fines. This exposes Bassetlaw to open-ended penalties for failure to meet Consumer Standards, which is particularly material given concurrent compliance pressures from Awaab's Law.
findings.matters: Unlimited regulatory fines represent a contingent liability that is not quantified and could materially affect the HRA if standards are breached.
findings.figures: Cap was £5,000; now unlimited.
findings.quote: Failure to deliver the RSH Consumer Standards puts the Council at risk of unlimited fines from the Regulator of Social Housing. This is significant because prior to this there was a cap of £5,000 for non-compliance.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Debt rising from £114.1m to £170.2m over five years, with £22.2m additional borrowing in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The HRA long-term debt is scheduled to grow substantially: from £114.119m at April 2026 to £136.325m at April 2027 (£22.2m new borrowing), £149.267m at April 2028 (£12.9m new), and £170.171m by April 2030. This represents 49% growth in the debt book in five years, funded by capital investment in housing stock.
findings.matters: Rapid debt accumulation combined with rising interest rates and breached affordability ratios creates refinancing risk when existing loans mature.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Loss of Right to Buy capital receipts removes £1.55m of capital funding source; difference funded by additional borrowing
findings.detail: Government policy changes from April 2026 mean Bassetlaw can no longer use Right to Buy receipts for any capital purpose on existing stock. In 2025/26, RTB receipts were estimated at £1.55m. From 2026/27 onwards, these receipts generate insufficient value to be useable for capital investment and will need to be spent on development or returned. The difference will be funded by additional borrowing.
findings.matters: A capital funding source being closed off forces the council to borrow more, increasing leverage and debt service costs at a time when affordability metrics are already tight.
findings.figures: 2025/26: £1.55m; 2026/27 onwards: zero useable receipts
findings.quote: From 2026/27 there will be no useable capital receipts for existing stock as the sales receipts will not generate enough for this. The loss of the capital receipts that can be used for any capital purpose means that the difference will need to be funded by additional borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Borrowing rates doubled from forecast — 5.57% in 2026/27 vs 3.5% assumed a year ago
findings.detail: The paper shows long-term borrowing rate assumptions have risen significantly. Rates were forecast at 3.5% a year ago; the current assumption is 5.57% for 2026/27, falling only slowly to 5.15% by April 2030. This 2.07 percentage point increase directly increases debt service costs across the entire 30-year plan.
findings.matters: Rate forecasts that deteriorate this sharply undermine the business plan's sensitivity analysis and suggest the assumptions underpinning affordability are not stable.
findings.figures: 3.5% assumed last year; 5.57% now assumed for 2026/27; 5.15% by April 2030
findings.quote: Borrowing rates are assumed to rise to 5.57% in 2026/27 and then fall slowly to 5.15% by 1 April 2030, but this was forecast to be 3.5% this time last year.

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Revenue reserves fall below minimum required balance from year 24 and become deeply negative by year 30
findings.detail: The 30-year reserves projection shows the HRA balance drops below the minimum target in year 24, then falls sharply negative: -£596k in year 27, -£2.768m in year 28, and -£13.406m by year 30. This is the reserve that should protect the HRA against cost shocks.
findings.matters: Negative reserves in the later years of a 30-year housing plan indicate the business model becomes unaffordable without further intervention, borrowing, or service cuts.
findings.quote: Balance at 31 March 2027 3,328 0' Surplus/(deficit) 697 0 ... Balance at 31 March 2030 (shown as -13,406 in breach table)

findings.paper_title: 2a - Report - Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-27 and future years to 2028-29
findings.headline: Interest cover ratio breaches the council's own affordability test in the first five years
findings.detail: The council adopted a 1.25x interest cover ratio as its measure of HRA affordability in 2024/25. The 30-year business plan shows this ratio is breached for the first five years of the forecast period, only improving to acceptable levels around year 15. This directly contradicts the council's stated solvency test.
findings.matters: A council breaching its own affordability threshold signals the business plan is fragile and dependent on assumptions that may not hold.
findings.figures: Interest cover ratio of 1.25x is the threshold; first five years breach this.
findings.quote: Whilst the interest cover ratios show that for the first five years of the plan, the interest cover ratio of 1.25 is breached the rate improves each year until around year 15.

findings.paper_title: 5b - Appendix 1 - BDC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Aurora Wellbeing Centre interest-free loan being converted to grant (principal loss)
findings.detail: The council holds a £120k interest-free loan to Aurora Wellbeing Centre which is being converted into a grant. This represents a direct loss of council principal. Additionally, Bersahill Limited holds a £3.5m non-treasury investment (property development loan), though £3.2m is expected to be repaid shortly. Both investments sit outside normal treasury management.
findings.matters: The Aurora conversion represents a loss of principal that will accelerate reserve depletion. The existence of non-treasury, non-commercial investments (especially interest-free lending) signals exposure to non-standard credit risks and suggests the council is willing to subordinate commercial terms to other objectives.
findings.figures: Aurora: £120k interest-free loan being converted to grant; Bersahill: £3.5m with £3.2m repayment expected
findings.quote: Aurora Wellbeing Centre – an interest free loan of £120k to the charitable organisation. which is in the process of being converted into a grant. Further details will be provided in due course.

findings.paper_title: 5b - Appendix 1 - BDC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Cumulative borrowing requirement of £95.9m over five years
findings.detail: The council will borrow £95.9m cumulatively to fund capital plans, comprising £66.6m in net financing needs plus £28.0m to refinance existing maturing loans. The Capital Financing Requirement grows from £180.5m to £216.4m, while the council maintains an under-borrowed position by using cash reserves rather than borrowing the full amount now.
findings.matters: The scale and trajectory of new borrowing directly affects debt burden and service affordability. Lenders assess whether the council can service this debt and whether the strategy of deferring borrowing (betting on interest rate falls) is prudent.
findings.figures: Total cumulative borrowing £95.9m (£66.6m net financing need + £28.0m refinancing); CFR grows from £180,496k to £216,397k
findings.quote: By the end of 2030/31, the Council will have an estimated cumulative borrowing requirement of £95.9m. This includes the cumulative net financing need over the five year period (£66.6m) and is additional to the refinancing of existing loans (£28.0m).

findings.paper_title: 5b - Appendix 1 - BDC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: General Fund reserves depleting 78% from £25.6m to £5.5m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's General Fund reserves are forecast to decline sharply over the five-year period. Starting at £25.6m in 2026/27, they fall to just £5.5m by 2030/31, a loss of £20.1m. This leaves minimal financial contingency by the end of the forecast period, reducing the council's ability to absorb unexpected shocks or demand changes.
findings.matters: A lender assesses financial resilience through reserve levels. Reserves falling to this level indicate the council will have very limited buffers against service pressures, spending overruns, or revenue shortfalls—a significant constraint on future borrowing capacity and financial flexibility.
findings.quote: Estimated Year End Resources (£000s) General Fund 25,631 ... 5,509

findings.paper_title: 6b - Appendix A - BDC Capital Investment Strategy and General Fund Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: HRA discount on PWLB borrowing (0.4%) is uncertain and may be withdrawn, which would increase debt servicing costs on £56M new HRA borrowing
findings.detail: The council notes that HRA borrowing attracts a 0.4% discount from PWLB rates, but states this is 'uncertain how long this will be extended for.' Loss of this discount would increase the annual cost of servicing the £56M HRA borrowing planned over the period.
findings.matters: Policy-driven changes to borrowing terms could significantly increase the council's financing costs and revenue burden, reducing budget flexibility and capacity to respond to other pressures.
findings.figures: PWLB long-term rates 4.7%-5.9%; HRA currently gets additional 0.4% discount; £22.206M HRA borrowing in 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: HRA borrowing is currently available from the PWLB at a further discount of 0.4%. It is uncertain how long this will be extended for.

findings.paper_title: 6b - Appendix A - BDC Capital Investment Strategy and General Fund Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Council explicitly states capital budgets may be insufficient due to construction inflation and demand-driven price rises
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that 'the approved budgets for projects may not be sufficient, resulting in challenges around affordability and value for money' due to high levels of demand across construction and transport markets plus continuing inflation impacts. This creates real risk of scheme overruns.
findings.matters: Cost inflation that cannot be absorbed within approved budgets could force the council to either borrow more than planned, reduce scheme scope, or cancel schemes, any of which indicates budget discipline problems.
findings.figures: Capital programme total £120.2M over 5 years; specific schemes (e.g. 73 Bridge St £3.1M, decarbonisation works £6.2M in pipeline)
findings.quote: The current environment for the delivery of the Capital Programme is extremely challenging due to high levels of demand across the construction and transport markets, as well as the continuing impact from recent high levels of inflation. This has meant that the approved budgets for projects may not be sufficient, resulting in challenges around affordability and value for money.

findings.paper_title: 6b - Appendix A - BDC Capital Investment Strategy and General Fund Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: General Fund 'already operates to very tight margins' yet is planning to borrow £5.8M in 2026/27 for capital with constrained revenue recovery
findings.detail: The council states unsupported prudential borrowing for General Fund will be 'tightly controlled due to the financial impact it will have on a revenue budget that already operates to very tight margins.' Financing costs as proportion of net revenue stream are negative in 2026/27-2027/28, becoming positive from 2029/30.
findings.matters: Tight revenue margins limit the council's ability to absorb unexpected cost increases or revenue shortfalls, creating risk that capital schemes could require re-prioritisation or that revenue budgets could be squeezed to service debt.
findings.figures: General Fund borrowing £5.790M in 2026/27; financing costs -1% of net revenue stream in 2026/27
findings.quote: For the General Fund, unsupported prudential borrowing will be tightly controlled due to the financial impact it will have on a revenue budget that already operates to very tight margins.

findings.paper_title: 6b - Appendix A - BDC Capital Investment Strategy and General Fund Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: HRA is borrowing 74% of its 2026/27 capital spend (£22.2M out of £30.1M), with further £56M HRA borrowing planned over five years for new housing
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is heavily dependent on borrowing to fund capital investment, with £22.2M borrowed in 2026/27 and total HRA borrowing of £56.1M across the five-year period for new housing developments. This creates significant ongoing revenue commitments.
findings.matters: HRA borrowing must be serviced from housing rents and is protected by the self-financing regime, but large-scale borrowing for new housing development increases revenue risk if occupancy or rent collection deteriorates.
findings.figures: HRA 2026/27: £22.206M borrowing out of £30.053M total expenditure; total HRA borrowing increase £56.1M over 5 years
findings.quote: Estimated HRA Capital Expenditure 30,053 [£000s]... Financed by Borrowing 22,206; A total of £13.5M has been approved in the HRA capital programme for building of new houses and refurbishment of existing properties the next 5 years.

findings.paper_title: 6b - Appendix A - BDC Capital Investment Strategy and General Fund Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement will increase by £63.5M over five years, with total CFR reaching £216.4M by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's cumulative outstanding debt is projected to rise significantly, from current levels to £216.4M by end of 2030/31. Of this increase, £56.1M relates to HRA new housing developments. The General Fund is funding £5.790M of its 2026/27 capital programme through borrowing despite tight revenue margins.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's total debt trajectory and capacity to service it, particularly when debt is growing faster than revenue capacity.
findings.figures: CFR increases by £63.5M; HRA contributes £56.1M of that increase; General Fund borrowing £5.790M in 2026/27
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase to £216.4M by the end of 2030/31, which equates to an increase of £63.5M. This is mainly due to the new housing developments within the HRA (£56.1M).

findings.paper_title: 5a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Audit Completion Report - year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Subsidiary S80 Limited remains without appointed auditors, described as a 'long-standing matter'
findings.detail: The council's subsidiary, S80 Limited, is required by law to have audited financial statements but has still not appointed an audit firm. The auditor flags this as a 'long-standing matter that the Audit Committee needs to be assured is addressed to comply with statutory reporting requirements.' No audit scope is possible for the subsidiary given the group disclaimer.
findings.matters: A subsidiary's accounts must be audited as part of group reporting. The council has failed to appoint auditors for its subsidiary, leaving that entity unaudited. This creates unknown financial exposure in the group accounts and represents a failure of basic governance.
findings.figures: S80 Limited - no appointed auditors assigned
findings.quote: The financial statement of S80 Limited are required to be audited, however the Council has still not appointed an audit firm. This has become a long-standing matter that the Audit Committee needs to be assured is addressed to comply with statutory reporting requirements.

findings.paper_title: 5a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Audit Completion Report - year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Audit could not be completed; insufficient working papers at start and quality issues persisted throughout
findings.detail: The audit began 1 September 2025 with only 73 of approximately 206 working paper requests (35%) received. A three-week pause was granted to allow papers to be prepared. When audit resumed, submissions had reached only 90%. Critical working papers including fixed asset register reconciliation and payroll reconciliation either remained outstanding or failed quality checks. The auditor concluded work could not be completed before the backstop date without compromising other audits.
findings.matters: The council was unable to provide adequate supporting documentation for an audit. This is a fundamental failure in financial reporting infrastructure and suggests the council may not have adequate systems to track and record its transactions accurately.
findings.figures: 73 of 206 working papers received at audit start (35%); increased to 90% after pause
findings.quote: At the start of the audit, 73 of approximately 206 working paper requests had been responded to. When the audit resumed, working paper submission had increased to around 90%, just short of the 100% that had been agreed. There were, however, ongoing issues with several key working papers—such as the reconciliation of the fixed asset register to the accounts and the payroll reconciliation—that were either still outstanding or did not meet the required quality threshold.

findings.paper_title: 5a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Audit Completion Report - year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Critical IT control deficiency: admin users can raise and self-approve purchase orders up to £10m and journals up to £100m with no audit trail
findings.detail: The auditor identified significant deficiencies in logical security controls. Users with admin access can raise AND approve their own purchase orders up to £10m with no possible way of tracking this activity. The same admin users can also raise and self-approve journals up to £100m. Additionally, password requirements fall below best practice (only 6 characters minimum) and no periodic user access reviews were performed during the year.
findings.matters: These control deficiencies create material risk of unauthorised or fraudulent transactions without detection. An admin user could theoretically move £100m via journal entries with full self-approval and no audit trail. This undermines the entire control environment for financial reporting.
findings.figures: Purchase orders: £10m self-approval limit; Journals: £100m self-approval limit
findings.quote: Users set up with 'Admin' access have the ability to raise and approve their own purchase orders up to £10m and there is no possible way of tracking this. Users set up with 'Admin' access can raise and self-approve journals up to £100m.

findings.paper_title: 5a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Audit Completion Report - year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Long-standing governance weakness in financial reporting dating back to 2020/21, unresolved after multiple audit recommendations
findings.detail: The auditor identified a significant weakness in arrangements for the council's statutory financial reporting in 2020/21. Recommendations were made to address underlying issues. Despite this, material errors and internal control weaknesses continued in 2021/22 with the same issues recurring. The weakness remains unaddressed in 2024/25, with draft accounts again containing material errors and insufficient quality control.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off issue: it is a systemic failure to maintain accurate financial reporting that has persisted across four financial years despite audit recommendations. This indicates management has failed to remediate fundamental governance over financial reporting.
findings.figures: Issues identified in 2020/21, 2021/22, and again in 2024/25
findings.quote: Our work on the 2020/21 financial statements took longer than would ordinarily be expected because of issues in preparation of the Council's draft statutory financial statements. Recommendations to address the underlying issues were raised as internal control weaknesses in the 2020/21 Audit Completion Report. Despite these recommendations being made, during the 2021/22 financial audit, material errors and internal control weaknesses have been identified, with a continuation of issues from 2020/21.

findings.paper_title: 5a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Audit Completion Report - year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Material error of £18.59m found in property revaluation, plus multiple uncorrected disclosure misstatements
findings.detail: A revaluation journal of £18.59m was posted as a downward movement instead of upward. Four additional disclosure misstatements were identified and not corrected by management: removal of non-material accounting policies, correction of banding in officers' remuneration note, missing depreciation charge on property/plant/equipment, and missing revaluation table amendments.
findings.matters: The council's own review processes failed to catch a £18.59m error in fixed asset valuation. Combined with uncorrected disclosure issues and the auditor's inability to complete their work, material inaccuracies may remain in the published accounts.
findings.quote: Dr: Property, Plant & Equipment 18,590 (£'000). Cr: Unusable Reserves/(Surplus) or Deficit on Revaluation (18,590). Correction of a revaluation journal that was posted as a downward revaluation movement instead of an upward revaluation movement.

findings.paper_title: 5a1 - Appendix 1 - BDC Audit Completion Report - year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Auditor issued disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 accounts, providing no assurance over financial statements
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars could not complete sufficient audit procedures before the 27 February 2026 backstop date imposed by the Accounts and Audit (Amendment) Regulations 2024. The council's 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts also have disclaimed opinions, meaning opening balances lack assurance across three consecutive years. This is the third consecutive year without an unqualified audit opinion.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on audited financial statements to understand council financial position. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor has not verified the accuracy of any figures or assertions in the accounts. Combined with two prior years of disclaimers, the council's financial position is unverified for three years.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: It has not been possible to complete sufficient procedures as part of the current year's audit to enable us to issue a non-disclaimed opinion. For this reason, we will be issuing a disclaimed opinion in time for the Council to publish its financial statements by the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Cyber security controls remain incomplete; Incident Response Plan still being finalized
news_drafts.lead: Cyber incidents could disrupt council operations, corrupt or expose financial data, and disrupt service delivery

news_drafts.headline: Procurement control weaknesses persist despite 2024/25 action marked complete; Partial Assurance audit rating issued
news_drafts.lead: Procurement control failures affect value for money, fraud risk, and proper use of public funds; the issue persisting despite being marked resolved suggests either incomplete remediation or recurring problems

news_drafts.headline: Two of four audit follow-up reviews in 2024/25 showed poor or little progress on implementing prior recommendations
news_drafts.lead: Non-implementation of audit recommendations indicates control gaps persist; weak follow-through on audit action plans is a red flag for governance quality
